what_it_does: Transformer-based AI language models keep a growing record of past tokens (pieces of text) called the key-value cache (KV cache) — think of it as the model's working notepad that it must consult every time it generates a new word. For very long documents (over one million tokens), this notepad becomes enormous and the bandwidth required to read it becomes the main bottleneck, not the arithmetic. This paper observes that not all notepad entries are equally relevant, and proposes a distance-based sparsity scheme (DIAS) that focuses attention only on nearby and a few globally important entries, skipping the rest, with an approximate fast-search method (graph-based top-K) to find the most relevant ones quickly. To handle the memory capacity problem, it also proposes a tree-shaped hardware architecture called TreePIM where the KV cache lives inside the memory chips themselves and simple arithmetic is performed there — reducing the amount of data that must travel on the bandwidth-limited bus between memory and processor. The exact accuracy trade-offs and hardware efficiency numbers are not available from the abstract.
